source: Raman, Lundy, Leyton-Brown (2025) Reasoning Models are Test Exploiters: Rethinking Multiple Choice
finding: Direct test of build-before-options for LLMs. 27 LLMs, 15 benchmarks, five formats. Reasoning over the options (QMC-CoT) beats free reasoning without options (Q-CoT). Reasoning only before seeing options (Q-CoT then pick) keeps MCQA a fair proxy for free-text skill.
numbers: Models above about 50B scored 30 to 40 points higher with options shown before CoT than without. Reasoning models are better exploiters. o3 reached 77.34% on Q-CoT; nearly all reasoning models above 90% on QMC-CoT. Open models on 5000 questions per dataset, o3 and gpt-4o on 1000.
quote: MCQA remained a good proxy ... as long as they were allowed to perform chain-of-thought reasoning only before being presented with the options
limits: Knowledge and math MCQA, not matrices. Free-text arm scored by exact match, so stricter than choosing. Two-stage arm reintroduces options to the same model, so reasoning models can still eliminate in stage 2. Accuracy is not at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of S3 build-first. Supports a scaffold rule: finish reasoning and commit a candidate answer before options are in view, and keep reasoning separate from selection.

source: Raman et al. (2025) Reasoning Models are Test Exploiters, NOTA and option-design experiments
finding: A none-of-the-above (NOTA) option cuts the elimination shortcut. Harder distractors do not reliably cut it and for some models raise it.
numbers: On options-only prompts reasoning models scored 12.63 points above non-reasoning models; with NOTA only 5.29 points above. Reasoning models chose NOTA 55.82% of the time versus 30.05% for non-reasoning (true rate 25%). With NOTA in the stage-2 option set, performance fell 2 to 15 points when the true answer was absent. MMLU-Pro (10 options) was usually harder to exploit than MMLU, but reasoning models still exploited it more than non-reasoning models.
limits: NOTA also makes models treat items as trick questions (seen in chains of thought). DeepSeek R1 70B NOTA precision 0.85 and recall 0.58 when NOTA was correct.
agent_relevance: Elimination is a real, measurable shortcut in strong reasoning models. Gives a cheap probe: add a NOTA slot and see if accuracy drops. Our S4 check should not rest on option patterns.

source: Balepur, Ravichander, Rudinger (2024) Artifacts or Abduction: How Do LLMs Answer Multiple-Choice Questions Without the Question?
finding: Choices-only prompts beat a majority baseline in 11 of 12 model-dataset cases (LLaMA-2, Falcon, Phi-2, Mixtral on ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag), with a gain up to 0.33 accuracy. Memorization alone does not explain it. Models seem to use how the choices relate to each other, and can sometimes infer a question close to the original (matched the original 42% of the time in one analysis).
numbers: 11/12 cases beat majority; up to 0.33 gain. Inferred-question analysis: 42% match to the original question.
limits: Older open models, 1-token prompting. Not reasoning models, not matrices. Shortcut size varies by dataset.
agent_relevance: Choice-only leakage is the LLM version of response elimination. It sets a floor: any matrix or MCQ accuracy must be compared with a choices-only baseline.

source: Balepur, Rudinger, Boyd-Graber (2025) Which of These Best Describes Multiple Choice Evaluation with LLMs? A) Forced B) Flawed C) Fixable D) All of the Above
finding: Position paper. Argues MCQA tests recognition rather than generation, has leakage and shortcuts, and proposes constructed-response formats plus scoring that penalises guessing, borrowed from education testing.
numbers: No new experiment; synthesis of earlier results.
limits: Opinion and review. Abstract and structure read, not every cited result.
agent_relevance: Supports the human-test parallel: constructed-response is the exam-side fix that Becker 2016 used on matrices. Agrees with build-first.

source: Balepur, Palta, Rudinger (2024) It's Not Easy Being Wrong: LLMs Struggle with Process of Elimination Reasoning
finding: Asking LLMs to reason toward the wrong option (elimination) did worse than reasoning toward the right option in every model and dataset. Agreement between the two strategies was lower than each strategy's own self-consistency. The gap narrowed as models got bigger.
numbers: 500 questions per dataset, two choices each, four datasets (CommonsenseQA, SIQA, ARC, OpenBookQA). Small models (7B, 13B) with elimination often fell below 50/50 guessing. GPT-3.5 on ARC: direct answer and elimination agreed 86.6 or 85.5 percent, versus self-consistency 97.5 or 97.0. CoT improved direct answer in 19 of 24 cases but not elimination (never for Falcon).
limits: Two-option questions only; GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, Falcon; no GPT-4 or reasoning models. Elimination forced into a single step.
agent_relevance: Forced pure elimination is weak for LLMs. Fits the human finding that pure elimination is rare and poor. Use elimination only as a check after a built answer.

source: Ma and Du (2023) POE: Process of Elimination for Multiple Choice Reasoning
finding: A two-step scorer (score options, mask the below-average ones, then choose) beat multiple-choice prompting zero-shot on 5 of 8 tasks and matched it on 3. The gain was biggest on logical tasks.
numbers: FLAN-T5-XL (3B), 100 items per task, 5 seeds. Logical Deduction MCP 39.8 vs POE 53.6; Conceptual Combinations 60.2 vs 72.2; CommonsenseQA 87.2 vs 89.2; SIQA 79.0 vs 82.0; ANLI 57.8 vs 55.0 (POE lower).
limits: Small model, 100 items per task, likelihood scoring rather than reasoning chains, ChatGPT test only partial. Elimination is soft masking, not hard pruning.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to d05: a soft eliminate-then-choose step can help. The order (score all, drop clearly wrong, then pick) is testable at equal tokens in S4.

source: Chandak, Goel, Prabhu, Hardt, Geiping (2025) Answer Matching Outperforms Multiple Choice for Language Model Evaluation
finding: Generate a free-form answer without the options, then match it to the reference. Agreement with human grading is near human inter-annotator level, while multiple choice agrees poorly. Model rankings change when scored on free-form answers.
numbers: Human-annotated MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond. Answer-matching alignment values around 0.89 to 0.97 (Scott's pi) in the text I read; the exact multiple-choice figure was not extracted.
limits: Evaluation paper, not a solving-strategy paper.
agent_relevance: A build-first answer can be checked against options by matching. In the agent, S4 can be a match step between the built answer and each option: a decoupled build and select.

source: Laurence and Macedo (2023) Cognitive strategies in matrix-reasoning tasks: State of the art (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 30:147-159)
finding: Review. Jarosz et al. (2019, think-aloud) found over 50% used constructive matching, only about 3% pure response elimination, and a hybrid called isolate-and-eliminate (find one rule, drop options that break it, find the next rule, repeat). Kucharsky et al. (2020) found no pure elimination cluster with unsupervised gaze methods, which fits elimination being a frustrated constructive matching. Becker 2016 constructed-response and Loesche 2015 rule training both reduced elimination.
numbers: Jarosz 2019: >50% constructive, 3% pure elimination. Vigneau 2006 four regression models explained 32%, 30%, 49%, 51% of Raven score.
limits: Review; every number is second-hand. Accuracy by strategy in Jarosz 2019 is not given.
agent_relevance: Gives the hybrid a definition that can be written as a fixed procedure: isolate a rule, prune options, repeat. Warns that pure elimination is a rare label.

source: Laurence, Mecca, Serpa, Martin, Macedo (2018) Eye Movements and Cognitive Strategy in a Fluid Intelligence Test: Item Type Analysis (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Rate of toggling was the best predictor of score on the WMT-2 matrix test, and all rule types followed the same strategy. The paper also gives a second-hand description of Bethell-Fox 1984.
numbers: N=34 adults, WMT-2. Toggle rate explained 45% of score variance; r between toggle rate and score -0.68 (p<.001); baseline pupil size unrelated to intelligence. Bethell-Fox 1984 as described: 28 subjects, geometric analogies A:B::C:?, multiple alternatives, fixation counts and sequences.
limits: Small N, one test, one lab. The Bethell-Fox description is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Toggle rate is the cleanest human index; its agent analogue is how often a trace flips between the problem and the option list.

source: Bethell-Fox, Lohman, Snow (1984) Adaptive reasoning: componential and eye movement analysis of geometric analogy performance (Intelligence 8:205-238)
finding: Could not be opened (paywalled, no open copy found). Secondary sources (Laurence 2018, Laurence and Macedo 2023) agree on the design: about 28 people, geometric analogies with multiple alternatives, eye tracking, fixation count and sequence; higher-ability people showed constructive matching and strategy depended on difficulty.
numbers: N=28 only, from Laurence 2018. No effect sizes and no switch-point boundary recovered.
limits: Gap 3 stays open. All claims about this paper stay second-hand.
agent_relevance: Do not cite effect sizes from this paper in the schema notes. Cite only the qualitative claim.

source: Liu, Man, Zhan (2024 preprint) Unveiling Cognitive Strategies: Clustering Eye-Tracking Measures in Computerized Matrix-Reasoning Tasks
finding: Clustering three gaze measures (proportional time on matrix, rate of toggling, relative latency to first toggle) gave two clusters on most items. The constructive cluster scored higher on almost every item, was the smaller cluster on every item, and constructive matching was used more on easier items.
numbers: 192 college students, APM 36 items (data from Liu et al. 2023). Number of items solved by constructive matching correlated r=0.31 (p<.01) with total score; correlation with mean response time r=-0.1 (p=.17).
limits: Preprint. Strategy label comes from gaze clusters, not checked by report. Same lab and data as the earlier Liu 2023 paper.
agent_relevance: Another gaze-labelled sign that strategy is chosen per item by difficulty, supporting an adaptive switch rather than a fixed strategy.

source: Haznitrama, Ardi, Oh (2026) A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities (NeuroCognition), arXiv 2603.02540 v2
finding: RAPM-style text items were given in 8-option multiple choice (MC) and in a generative format (Gen, free-form string). Format changed accuracy, in opposite directions across models. This is the source of the Claude Sonnet 4 / GPT-5 reversal in gap 8.
numbers: Text MC to Gen: GPT-5 0.540 to 0.605, Claude Sonnet 4 0.560 to 0.385, Grok 4 Fast 0.690 to 0.555. Humans (N=9 pilot, 15 items per format): 0.430 MC, 0.444 Gen; human image RAPM 0.814 (from another study).
limits: Single run per model, N=9 humans, 15 items per format, text version of items. Reasoning was disabled for Claude Sonnet 4 on RAPM. Differences not tested model by model.
agent_relevance: No single direction; the effect is model-specific. Gap 8 is located, not replicated: one paper, no repeat runs.

source: Haznitrama et al. (2026) NeuroCognition, ablation on reasoning and hints
finding: Switching reasoning off helped on text multiple choice and did nothing detectable on text generation or image items. Pattern hints gave no average gain. Authors say long chains of thought get confused by distractors in 8-choice items, while generation benefits from reasoning to build a coherent answer.
numbers: Reasoning off: Text MC gain p=.021; Text Gen p=.83 (n.s.); Image MC p=.173 (n.s.). Pattern hints: Text MC p=.177, Text Gen p=.45, Image MC p=.666, none significant. Trace failures: hallucinated features, over-reading complex rules (symmetry grids) instead of XOR or concatenation, and in Gen a mismatch between the right attribute rules and the string produced.
limits: Only models where reasoning can be switched off. Mixed set of models, one run each.
agent_relevance: With options in view, reasoning chains drift toward distractors, so S3 build-first should keep options out of the chain. A built answer also needs a rule-to-answer consistency check (the Gen failure).

source: Urgun and Ari (2025) An Analysis of Architectural Impact on LLM-based Abstract Visual Reasoning: RAVEN-FAIR benchmark
finding: Models were given no answer choices and had to generate the answer image through JSON extraction, LLM reasoning and a drawing tool. Four architectures (single-shot, repetition, self-reflection, multi-agent) on GPT-4.1-Mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Gemini-1.5-Flash, Llama-3.3-70b. GPT-4.1-Mini best across architectures; multi-agent not uniformly beneficial.
numbers: Scored with SSIM and LPIPS, not accuracy. Abstract and first page only; no per-model numbers recorded.
limits: Abstract-level only. Image-similarity metrics, older small models.
agent_relevance: A build-only arm exists for matrices but is not compared with an elimination arm. Added structure (multi-agent) did not reliably help.

source: Jarosz, Raden, Wiley (2019) Working memory capacity and strategy use on the Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (Intelligence 77)
finding: Search-result summary only: think-aloud found a third hybrid strategy (isolate-and-eliminate) beside constructive matching and response elimination. Strategy use partly mediated the working-memory to score link. Constructive matching fell as items got harder.
numbers: No accuracy-by-strategy figure obtained. Share figures (over 50% constructive, 3% pure elimination) come from d08.
limits: Not opened. Gap 4 accuracy-by-strategy remains unanswered.
agent_relevance: The hybrid is frequent in humans, so a fixed isolate-prune-repeat procedure is a plausible S3 to S4 loop, but no human data here show it beats pure build.

source: Search coverage note (2026-11-10): no study found that compares build-first and elimination for reasoning-model agents on matrices
finding: Two WebSearch queries plus arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar probes (the APIs were mostly rate-limited) found no paper that runs generate-then-match against option elimination on matrices for current reasoning models, and none that measures trace metrics such as tokens before the first option mention. Closest are d01 (knowledge MCQA), d12 (text RAPM format swap) and d05 and d06 (elimination prompts).
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited, throttled search.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5 and 6 are open research questions for our own benchmark, not literature questions.
